sections.history: Tiruaappadi, today called Thiruvaippadi, is a village near Tiruppanandal in the Thiruvidaimarudur taluk of Thanjavur district. The hymns of Appar praise the Lord of Tiruaappadi, and the temple is reckoned the fortieth Shiva shrine on the northern bank of the Kaveri sung in the Tevaram. The village name is traced to aa, the cow, and paadi, the pasture, for this was grazing land where cattle were tended. Local accounts say the temple was rebuilt in stone in the Chola period and later extended by Pandya and Vijayanagara patrons; inscriptions are said to call the Lord Chokka Kooththar, Natarajar and Thiru Aappadi Udayar. The shrine is also honoured as the place where the Nayanar Chandesa attained his final union with Shiva.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and is enclosed by two corridors. It has no towering rajagopuram, but is entered through a graceful arched gateway. The front mandapam is built in the vavval nethi style, its roof said to resemble a bat's forehead, and is said to date from about the fifteenth century. The goddess Periyanayaki is honoured in a south-facing shrine to the right of the sanctum, and shrines of Bhairava, Surya and Sani stand in the great hall. Chandikeswarar is honoured close to the sanctum, as at every Shiva temple. In the south-west corner of the inner enclosure an athi tree, a sacred fig, stands over a linga and is believed to mark the place where Chandesa worshipped. The sacred waters of the shrine are linked with the river Manni, which flows nearby.
sections.legends: Visarasarman, a young brahmin, was entrusted with tending the village's cattle. Watching the cows, he saw how freely they gave their milk when they came to the riverbank, and in his heart he longed to offer it to the Lord. Beneath an athi tree beside the river Manni he shaped a linga from the river sand and bathed it with the cows' milk each day. Villagers, troubled to see good milk poured away, told his father. The father came to the bank in anger and kicked over the pots of milk; the boy, absorbed in worship and grieved at the insult to the Lord, struck out at him. Shiva, moved by a love so complete, appeared before the boy, took him as his own, and raised him to the rank of Chandesa, chief among his devotees, placing on him the garland he himself wore. From this the temple's name is explained: the Lord who delighted in the offering of milk is Paalugandha Eswarar, the one who relishes milk. Local tradition also tells of a cowherd whose daily milk spilled in secret at one spot until villagers dug there and uncovered a linga, which they installed and worshipped with milk. The place is also believed to be where the Nayanar attained liberation.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are the principal observances. The Brahmotsavam of Chandikeswarar is reported on the new-moon day after Maha Shivaratri, around February to March. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil lunar calendar.
sections.experience: Tiruaappadi is a small village shrine, best visited slowly in the quiet of morning or evening. Enter through the arched gateway, offer worship to Paalugandha Eswarar, then to Periyanayaki in her own shrine. Walk to the athi tree in the south-west of the inner enclosure and recall the boy who made a linga of river sand; an offering of milk is held especially fitting here. The temple is dear to those who seek the grace of Chandikeswarar. It lies only 2.5 km from Tiruppanandal, and the two shrines make an easy pairing.

visit.timings: Reported as open for a short period in the morning and again in the evening; listings differ, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruaappadi (Thiruvaippadi) lies on the Kumbakonam–Anaikarai route, about 2.5 km from Tiruppanandal and roughly 17 to 18 km from Kumbakonam, which has the nearest major railway station. The temple is set back from the main road, so take an auto-rickshaw from Tiruppanandal for the last stretch. Tiruchirappalli, the nearest major airport, is about 100 km away (approximate).
